column2: a friend says they broke the window only because they are scared of being punished
column3: know that fear of trouble is the most common reason people lie; owning up early usually makes the trouble smaller
column4: a lie often has to be covered by more lies, and getting caught makes things worse than the mistake itself

column2: a classmate says they have a pony and a pool at home to sound impressive
column3: understand that some people lie to be liked or admired; you can like them for who they really are
column4: wanting to fit in is natural, but friendships built on made-up stories feel shaky when the truth comes out

column2: a child says they already did their homework so they can play video games
column3: know that lying to get something you want is still lying, even if the thing seems small
column4: the truth usually comes out, and then you lose both the game time and people's trust

column2: a sibling says "Mum said I could" when she did not
column3: check with the adult yourself before going along with it
column4: using an adult's name in a lie is a trick to make the lie hard to argue with

column2: a friend lies to cover for another friend who did something wrong
column3: know that loyalty does not mean lying for someone; you can stay kind to a friend without covering up harm
column4: covering up can let the harm continue and drags you into the trouble too

column2: someone pretends they understood the lesson because they feel embarrassed to ask
column3: know that saying "I don't understand" is honest and brave; teachers want to know
column4: pretending to understand means you miss the help you need

column2: a little brother of four says a dragon ate his biscuits
column3: know that very young children mix up pretend and real; this is imagination, not a wicked lie
column4: small children are still learning the difference between wishing, pretending and what really happened

column2: you tell a made-up story at story time about a talking dog
column3: know that telling a story everyone knows is made up is not lying
column4: lying means trying to make someone believe something false; fiction, plays and games of pretend are shared make-believe

column2: an actor plays a villain in a film
column3: know that actors are not lying; everyone knows it is a performance
column4: a lie needs the intention to fool someone into a false belief, and the audience is not fooled about what a film is

column2: someone lies so often that they do it even when there is no need
column3: understand that lying can become a habit, and habits can be changed with practice and help
column4: small lies make the next lie easier, and so does small honesty make the next truth easier

column2: your friend says "I've told you a million times!"
column3: know that this is exaggeration for effect (hyperbole), not a real number
column4: people use big numbers to show strong feeling, and listeners understand it is not meant literally

column2: a kid says they were sick when they really just did not want to go to a party
column3: know there are honest polite ways to say no, like "Thanks, but I can't come"
column4: you do not owe everyone a reason, so you rarely need to invent one

column2: Grandma gives you a jumper you don't like and asks if you like it
column3: thank her warmly for the thought and the effort, for example "Thank you, it's so cosy and you remembered my favourite colour"
column4: you can be honest about what you truly appreciate without hurting someone who tried to be kind

column2: a friend shows you a drawing and asks if it is good
column3: say something true and kind, like what you like about it, and maybe one gentle idea
column4: honest encouragement helps people improve and keeps your word trustworthy

column2: someone has a new haircut you don't like
column3: you do not have to give your opinion; say "It looks different, do you like it?" or nothing about it
column4: not every opinion needs to be said, and kind silence is not a lie

column2: your aunt's cooking does not taste nice to you
column3: say "Thank you for making dinner" and eat what you can politely
column4: thanking someone for their effort is true and kind; announcing you dislike the food at the table hurts feelings

column2: a friend's pet died and they ask if it was their fault when it wasn't
column3: tell them honestly it was not their fault and that you are sorry
column4: a comforting truth is the best kind of kindness

column2: you are planning a surprise party and the birthday child asks what you are doing on Saturday
column3: it is fine to keep the surprise, for example "Nothing special, why?" or "It's a secret!"
column4: a surprise is a happy secret that will be revealed soon and is meant to make the person glad

column2: a friend asks if you like their singing and they plan to sing at the talent show tomorrow
column3: be kind but honest, like "You're brave to do it, maybe practise the high part once more"
column4: a false "it's perfect" now might lead to embarrassment later, and gentle honesty helps

column2: someone asks you about something private you do not want to share
column3: you can say "I'd rather not talk about that"
column4: keeping private things private is your right and is not lying

column2: a younger child believes in the tooth fairy or Father Christmas
column3: do not spoil it for them; leave it to their family
column4: families decide how they handle these traditions, and older children can play along kindly

column2: you think a classmate's lunch smells odd
column3: keep the comment to yourself
column4: food comes from different cultures and families, and remarks about it can make someone ashamed

column2: a friend asks if you had fun at their party and you were a bit bored
column3: say what was true and good, like "Thanks for inviting me, the cake was great"
column4: you can choose kind true words instead of a hurtful truth or a big lie

column2: your parent asks if you like their new car and you don't care much
column3: a simple "It's nice, I like the colour" is fine
column4: small kindness about matters of taste does no harm

column2: you are asked to keep quiet about a friend's crush
column3: keeping it is kind and fine
column4: a harmless secret shared in trust should be respected

column2: someone asks how old a lady is and she seems uncomfortable
column3: do not press or repeat the question
column4: some people find age or weight private, and respecting that is polite

column2: you broke something and are tempted to say your sister did it
column3: never blame someone else for what you did
column4: blaming an innocent person hurts them twice: they get punished and they lose trust in you

column2: someone says a classmate stole money when they don't know it
column3: never accuse someone of something you have not seen and cannot prove
column4: a false accusation can damage a person's name for a long time

column2: a child tells a teacher a lie to get another child in trouble
column3: know this is a serious wrong; if you did it, tell the truth quickly
column4: it is unfair, it can lead to real punishment for someone innocent, and it destroys trust

column2: someone lies about being hurt to get attention
column3: know that false alarms make it harder for people to be believed later
column4: this is the lesson of "The Boy Who Cried Wolf": when he really needed help nobody came

column2: a child lies to a doctor about how they got hurt because they are scared
column3: tell doctors and nurses the truth about what happened
column4: doctors need true facts to treat you properly, and they are there to help, not to punish

column2: a child hides a bad school report from parents
column3: show it and talk about it
column4: parents and teachers can only help with problems they know about

column2: you lie about where you are going after school
column3: always tell your parents or carers the truth about where you are and who you are with
column4: if something goes wrong, they need to know where to find you

column2: a friend lies about their age to join an online game or app
column3: know that age limits (often 13 in the USA, UK, Australia and elsewhere) exist to protect children
column4: the rules are there because such sites may show content or contacts not safe for children

column2: someone says they swallowed medicine pills as a joke
column3: never joke about poisoning, swallowing things or being hurt; if it is true tell an adult at once
column4: adults must take such words seriously, and a joke can cause panic or a real emergency can be ignored

column2: a child makes a fake call to an emergency number for fun
column3: never prank call 911, 999, 112, 000 or 111
column4: it ties up help that someone in a real emergency needs, and it is against the law

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: a friend won't look you in the eye while telling a story
column3: know that avoiding eye contact does NOT prove a lie; shy, nervous or autistic people may do it while telling the truth
column4: there is no single body sign of lying, so judging by looks alone is unfair

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: a classmate's story keeps changing each time they tell it
column3: notice that changing details can be a sign the story is not true, but ask gently instead of accusing
column4: people do forget details, so changes are a clue to check, not proof

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: someone swears "cross my heart" or "on my mother's life"
column3: know that swearing harder does not make a statement more true
column4: a liar can swear just as easily as an honest person; facts are what count

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: a boy says he caught a fish as big as a car
column3: recognise exaggeration and take it with a smile
column4: fishing stories are famous for growing; people enlarge things to make a story exciting

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: a story sounds too perfect and full of amazing details
column3: ask simple questions or check another way before believing it
column4: unusual claims need good evidence

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: your friend claims to have met a famous footballer
column3: it might be true; you can ask for details or just enjoy the story
column4: being curious is fine, but calling someone a liar without proof is unkind

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: someone gets angry and changes the subject when asked a simple question
column3: notice it, but remember they may be upset for other reasons
column4: feelings can come from many places, so stay calm and fair

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: you see a lie-detector machine in a film
column3: know that real lie detectors (polygraphs) are not reliable and are not allowed as proof in many courts
column4: they measure nervousness like heartbeat and sweat, and honest people get nervous too

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: in a story, Pinocchio's nose grows when he lies
column3: know that real noses do not grow; it is a story to teach honesty
column4: there is no magic sign of a lie, which is why trust matters so much

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: a friend says they were at home when you saw them at the park
column3: ask kindly "I thought I saw you at the park?" and listen to the answer
column4: you might have been mistaken, and a calm question gives them a chance to explain or be honest

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: two friends tell you different versions of a fight
column3: listen to both and, if it matters, ask an adult to help sort it out
column4: people often remember events in their own favour without meaning to lie

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: a younger child insists they did not eat the chocolate but has chocolate on their face
column3: stay gentle and help them tell the truth
column4: young children often lie out of fear, and kindness makes honesty easier

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: you yourself remember an event differently from your parent
column3: know that memory can be wrong even when nobody is lying
column4: memory fills gaps by guessing, so honest people can disagree

column1: telling when someone may be lying
column2: someone uses "trust me" a lot
column3: judge by what people do over time, not by how often they say "trust me"
column4: trust is earned by actions, not by words alone

column2: a friend asks you to pinky promise
column3: only promise what you really mean to do
column4: a pinky promise is still a promise, and people remember broken ones

column2: you promised to come to a friend's game but now you are ill
column3: tell them as early as you can and say sorry
column4: a promise you cannot keep should be explained quickly so the other person is not left waiting

column2: someone asks you to promise something you are not sure you can do
column3: say "I'll try my best" instead of "I promise"
column4: honest uncertainty is better than a promise that will be broken

column2: you promised your parents to look after a new pet
column3: feed, water and clean up after it every day, even when you are busy
column4: an animal depends on you, and keeping this promise shows you can be trusted with more

column2: you promise to return a borrowed book by Friday
column3: return it on time and in the same condition
column4: keeping small promises is how people learn they can rely on you

column2: a friend makes you promise not to tell, then says someone is hurting them
column3: tell a trusted adult anyway; a promise to keep someone in danger is not one you have to keep
column4: keeping someone safe is more important than a promise

column2: your parent promised a trip to the zoo but it was cancelled
column3: tell them how you feel calmly and ask when you might go instead
column4: grown-ups sometimes cannot keep promises because things change, and talking helps

column2: an older child makes you promise something by threatening you
column3: tell an adult; a promise made under threat does not count
column4: promises must be made freely; pressure and threats are not fair

column2: you promised to play with one friend but another invites you somewhere more exciting
column3: keep your first promise or ask the first friend honestly if you can change plans
column4: dropping someone for a better offer hurts and they will remember

column2: you said "I promise I'll tidy my room later" just to stop being asked
column3: do it, or do not promise in the first place
column4: empty promises teach others your word means nothing

column2: you promised a younger sibling you would help build a model
column3: keep it even though it seems small to you
column4: younger children take promises very seriously and look up to you

column2: you forgot a promise completely
column3: own up, say sorry and fix it as soon as you can
column4: forgetting happens, and making it right shows you still care

column2: you promised to keep a friend's diary safe
column3: keep it safe and do not read it
column4: being trusted with something private is a promise in itself

column2: a friend says "promise you'll never be friends with her"
column3: you do not have to make that kind of promise
column4: promises that control who you can be friends with are not fair

column2: you peek while counting in hide-and-seek
column3: close your eyes and count properly
column4: the game is only fun when everyone plays by the same rules

column2: a friend moves an extra square in a board game when they think no one is looking
column3: say calmly "I think you went one too many, let's count again"
column4: pointing it out calmly keeps the game fair without starting a fight

column2: someone changes the rules halfway through because they are losing
column3: agree on rules before the game starts and stick to them
column4: changing rules to win is cheating, and it spoils the game for others

column2: you are the banker in Monopoly and could slip yourself extra money
column3: handle the bank honestly
column4: being trusted with the money is a test of honesty even in a game

column2: you are tagged in a game of tag but say you weren't
column3: admit it and become "it"
column4: games rely on players being honest about what happened

column2: you use a cheat code in a single-player video game
column3: know it is your choice in a game only you play, but do not claim scores made with cheats
column4: cheats in your own game harm nobody, but showing them off as real is lying

column2: someone offers you a hack to win in an online game
column3: do not use hacks or cheat programs online
column4: it is unfair to other players, breaks the rules, can get your account banned and often hides viruses

column2: you lose a game and feel like throwing the pieces
column3: take a breath, say "good game" and try again
column4: everyone loses sometimes; good losers are people others want to play with

column2: an older sibling lets a little one win at a game
column3: know that letting a small child win sometimes is kind, not cheating
column4: it keeps the game fun for someone just learning, and everyone knows the reason

column2: a player pretends to be fouled in football to win a free kick
column3: play fairly and do not fake falls (diving)
column4: faking is cheating and can get a yellow card; sport is about real skill

column2: your team wins because the referee missed a handball by your player
column3: it is honest and sporting to own up if asked
column4: fair play matters more than one goal, and people respect honest players

column2: a friend keeps winning card games by looking at your cards
column3: hold your cards close and say kindly that peeking isn't fair
column4: naming the problem lets the friend stop without a big argument

column2: the person next to you in a test has their answers showing
column3: keep your eyes on your own paper
column4: copying is cheating and the test is to find out what you know so the teacher can help you

column2: a friend asks to copy your homework
column3: offer to explain how you did it instead
column4: copying does not help them learn, and both of you can get in trouble

column2: you find the answers at the back of the textbook
column3: use them only to check your work after you have tried
column4: copying answers skips the learning the homework is meant to give

column2: your parent offers to do your school project for you
column3: ask them to help you, not to do it
column4: teachers want to see your work, and you learn by doing

column2: you are tempted to ask an AI chatbot to write your homework
column3: follow your school's rules; use tools only to help you understand, not to do the work for you
column4: handing in work you did not do is cheating and you miss the learning

column2: you copy sentences from a website into your report
column3: write in your own words and say where you found the facts
column4: copying someone else's writing as your own is called plagiarism and is a form of cheating

column2: you write spelling words on your hand before a test
column3: do not bring hidden notes into a test
column4: it is cheating, and the practice of learning the words is the real point

column2: you forge a parent's signature on a note or reading log
column3: never sign for a parent
column4: forging a signature is a serious lie and breaks trust with both school and family

column2: you fill in a reading log with books you did not read
column3: log only what you really read
column4: false records hide the truth from teachers who want to help you read better

column2: in a group project one child does nothing but wants their name on it
column3: tell the teacher kindly and honestly how the work was shared
column4: fair credit matters and teachers can help sort it out

column2: you see a classmate cheating in a test
column3: you can tell the teacher privately afterwards if it worries you
column4: it is unfair to the honest students, and a quiet word is better than a public scene

column2: you get a better mark than you deserve because the teacher added wrong
column3: tell the teacher about the mistake
column4: honesty about mistakes that help you shows real integrity

column2: you hear that a classmate "likes" someone
column3: do not pass it on
column4: rumours about crushes can embarrass people badly and spread fast

column2: a friend tells you something bad about another child
column3: ask "How do you know that?" and do not repeat it
column4: many rumours are untrue or twisted, and repeating them makes you part of the harm

column2: you play the game "Telephone" (Chinese whispers) and the message changes completely
column3: remember this when you hear rumours
column4: messages change each time they are passed on, so second-hand stories are often wrong

column2: there is a rumour that school will be closed tomorrow
column3: check with a teacher, the school website or your parents
column4: rumours like this are often false, and acting on them can get you in trouble

column2: someone spreads a rumour about you
column3: stay calm, tell the truth to people who matter, and tell a trusted adult if it is hurting you
column4: reacting angrily can make rumours spread more; adults can help stop them

column2: a group chat starts making fun of a classmate
column3: do not join in; leave the chat or tell an adult
column4: online gossip spreads fast, stays around and can really hurt someone

column2: a friend shows you a screenshot of someone's private messages
column3: do not share it further
column4: private messages were meant for one person, and spreading them betrays trust

column2: a new kid arrives and people whisper about them
column3: get to know them yourself and make up your own mind
column4: first rumours about new people are often wrong and make them feel lonely

column2: someone says a teacher is "mean" or has a secret
column3: judge people by how they treat you, not by gossip
column4: stories about adults are often invented or exaggerated

column2: you are tempted to tell a juicy secret to look interesting
column3: keep it to yourself
column4: being a person who keeps secrets makes people trust you more than being the one with gossip

column2: you realise a rumour you passed on was untrue
column3: go back to those you told and say it was not true, and say sorry to the person
column4: correcting a rumour helps undo the harm

column2: a rumour says a scary character will come to school
column3: know these viral "challenge" or scary character rumours are usually hoaxes; tell an adult if you are frightened
column4: adults can check whether there is any real danger and can reassure you

column2: friends whisper and giggle while looking at someone
column3: do not join in whispering about people who are present
column4: it makes the person feel left out and talked about

column2: someone talks about another child's family problems
column3: do not spread news about other people's families
column4: family troubles are private and gossip can make a hard time worse

column2: you tell a joke and nobody laughs
column3: laugh it off and try another time
column4: humour is about the moment and the people; not every joke lands

column2: someone says something mean then adds "just joking"
column3: know that "just joking" does not make a hurtful remark okay; you can say "That wasn't funny to me"
column4: a joke is only a joke if everyone, including the target, can laugh

column2: a classmate tells a joke about someone's race, religion or disability
column3: do not laugh; say it isn't okay or tell a teacher
column4: jokes that mock who people are cause real hurt and spread prejudice

column2: you and a friend share an inside joke in front of others
column3: include others or explain it
column4: inside jokes can make others feel left out

column2: someone uses sarcasm, saying "Great weather!" in pouring rain
column3: know that sarcasm means the opposite of the words and is shown by tone
column4: it is a kind of joke, not a lie, because the speaker expects you to understand

column2: you laugh at a friend who slipped and hurt themselves
column3: first check if they are okay
column4: laughing at someone hurt can feel cruel, while laughing together later is fine if they find it funny too

column2: knock-knock jokes with a younger sibling
column3: play along and laugh even if it is silly
column4: sharing jokes builds friendship and helps younger children learn language

column2: you make a joke about bombs or weapons at an airport or school
column3: never joke about bombs, weapons or threats
column4: staff must treat such words seriously, and it can cause alarm, searches and serious trouble

column2: a friend calls you a funny nickname you both like
column3: friendly nicknames are fine when both people enjoy them
column4: teasing between friends can be a sign of closeness when it is kind

column2: someone keeps calling a classmate a name they hate
column3: stop if it is you; if it is others, tell them it isn't nice or tell an adult
column4: teasing that hurts and goes on is bullying

column2: you are teased about your glasses, braces or freckles
column3: say "Stop, I don't like that" calmly and walk away; tell an adult if it continues
column4: teasing about how people look hurts and is never your fault

column2: someone teases a classmate about their accent or the language they speak at home
column3: stand up for them or stay with them
column4: speaking more than one language is a skill, and mocking accents is unkind

column2: you tease someone and they say "stop"
column3: stop at once, even if you think it is still funny
column4: stop means the fun is over for them, and respecting it keeps the friendship safe

column2: tickling a friend who says stop
column3: stop immediately when anyone says stop or tries to get away
column4: tickling can feel bad and frightening when you cannot escape, and "stop" must always be respected

column2: someone hides a classmate's bag as a joke and they get upset
column3: give it back and say sorry
column4: jokes that make someone worried or late are not fun for them

column2: teasing about someone's weight or body
column3: never tease about bodies or food
column4: it can hurt for years and lead to eating problems

column2: someone posts a funny photo of a friend online without asking
column3: always ask before posting photos of other people
column4: what goes online can stay there and be seen by many people

column2: an older sibling teases you constantly
column3: tell them how it makes you feel, and ask a parent for help if it continues
column4: parents can help siblings learn where the line is

column2: you are not sure if teasing has gone too far
column3: look at the other person's face and ask "Are you okay with this?"
column4: the other person's feelings decide whether it is still fun

column2: someone teases a boy for liking dancing or a girl for liking football
column3: do not join in; everyone can like what they like
column4: teasing about interests limits people and makes them hide what they enjoy

column2: a friend wants to pull a chair away as someone sits down
column3: never do it
column4: the person can fall and badly hurt their back or head

column2: a whoopee cushion on a friend's seat
column3: a harmless prank is fine when the person will laugh too
column4: good pranks make everyone laugh, including the person pranked, and harm no one

column2: putting salt in the sugar bowl
column3: think about who will be fooled and whether they will be upset or waste food
column4: a prank that spoils someone's food or day is not funny to them

column2: jumping out to scare someone
column3: be careful with scare pranks, never near stairs, roads or with someone who is frail or has a heart condition
column4: a fright can make people fall or feel unwell

column2: a fake spider or rubber snake in a drawer
column3: avoid it with people who are truly afraid of spiders or snakes
column4: for someone with a real fear, it can cause panic rather than fun

column2: making a prank phone call to a stranger
column3: do not prank call people
column4: it can scare or annoy them, especially older people living alone

column2: a friend wants to film a prank to post online
column3: do not prank people for videos without their agreement
column4: being laughed at by many people online can be very humiliating

column2: a prank that damages things, like egging a house or stuffing a toilet
column3: never damage property in a prank
column4: someone has to clean or pay for it, and it can be a crime

column2: a prank on a pet, like scaring the dog or cat
column3: never prank animals
column4: animals do not understand jokes; they get frightened, stressed or hurt

column2: ringing doorbells and running away ("knock down ginger" or "ding dong ditch")
column3: do not do it
column4: it can frighten people, and running away near roads is dangerous

column2: a prank goes wrong and someone cries
column3: stop, say sorry and help them
column4: a prank that hurts someone is no longer a joke, and making it right matters

column2: pranking a teacher
column3: keep it very gentle, or skip it
column4: teachers are people too, and a prank that disrupts the class or embarrasses them can lead to trouble

column2: pranking someone with food they are allergic to
column3: never trick anyone about what is in their food
column4: food allergies can kill, and hiding ingredients is dangerous

column2: hiding a friend's shoes before they go home
column3: do not hide things people need
column4: they could be late, get in trouble or be really worried

column2: April 1st arrives and you want to trick your family
column3: play gentle, harmless tricks and say "April Fool!" quickly
column4: the fun of April Fools' Day is the shared laugh, not making people feel stupid

column2: in the UK and Ireland someone plays an April Fool trick in the afternoon
column3: know the tradition there is that tricks should be done before midday; whoever pranks after noon is the "fool"
column4: it is a playful custom that keeps the joking to the morning

column2: in Scotland April Fools' Day is called "Hunt the Gowk"
column3: know a "gowk" is a cuckoo, meaning a fool, and people are sent on silly errands
column4: different places have their own versions of the same playful tradition

column2: a news website reports something silly on April 1st
column3: check the date and think about whether it is a joke
column4: news and companies often publish joke stories on April Fools' Day, such as the famous 1957 BBC report of spaghetti growing on trees

column2: someone tells you on April 1st that school is cancelled
column3: check with an adult before believing it
column4: big news on April 1st is often a joke

column2: a friend gets upset by your April Fool trick
column3: say sorry and tell them the truth at once
column4: the joke is over as soon as someone is hurt

column2: an April Fool trick involves a fake injury or emergency
column3: never pretend to be hurt, missing or in danger as a joke
column4: it causes real fear and can waste emergency services' time

column2: you are fooled on April Fools' Day
column3: laugh along and maybe plan a gentle trick for next year
column4: being a good sport is part of the fun

column2: a magician makes a coin disappear
column3: know it is sleight of hand: quick, practised hand movements you don't notice
column4: magic tricks are skill and practice, not real magic

column2: a magician says "Look at this hand!" while the other hand does something
column3: learn the word misdirection: steering attention away from the secret move
column4: our attention is limited, so we miss things we are not looking at

column2: a magician guesses the card you chose
column3: know they may have "forced" the card or seen it secretly
column4: magicians use clever methods to make choices seem free when they are not

column2: you learn a magic trick and a friend begs to know the secret
column3: it is fine to keep the secret; magicians traditionally do not reveal how tricks are done
column4: the surprise is what makes the trick fun to watch

column2: you see a person "sawn in half" on stage
column3: know it uses a special box and two people or hidden spaces; nobody is hurt
column4: stage illusions use boxes, mirrors and hidden helpers

column2: magic tricks with fire, knives or swallowing things on video
column3: never copy dangerous tricks
column4: performers are trained and use special equipment; copying can cause serious injury

column2: a "psychic" says they can read minds
column3: know that mind-reading acts use tricks, like reading clues and guesses that fit many people
column4: no one has shown real mind-reading in fair scientific tests

column2: a fortune teller or horoscope tells your future
column3: enjoy it as fun if you like, but do not make real decisions based on it
column4: general statements fit almost anyone, and there is no evidence they can predict the future

column2: two lines with arrow ends look different lengths but are equal (the Müller-Lyer illusion)
column3: measure them with a ruler
column4: our brain can be fooled by surroundings, so measuring gives the true answer

column2: a straw in a glass of water looks bent
column3: know it is light bending (refraction) when it passes from water to air
column4: the straw is straight; light just changes direction

column2: the moon looks huge near the horizon
column3: know it is an illusion; the moon is about the same size in the sky all night
column4: the brain compares it with trees and buildings and judges it bigger

column2: on a hot road you see "water" ahead that vanishes
column3: know it is a mirage made by hot air bending light from the sky
column4: it is a real trick of light, not water

column2: a picture shows a duck or a rabbit depending on how you look
column3: know one image can be seen in two ways
column4: the brain chooses an interpretation, which shows that seeing is partly guessing

column2: a magician asks you to help on stage
column3: have fun and play along; it is safe for a professional show
column4: magicians plan audience help carefully, and you can say no if you don't want to

column2: an advert shows a toy flying and doing amazing things
column3: know adverts show toys at their best, sometimes with effects; read "pictures are for illustration"
column4: the real toy may be smaller or do less than it seems

column2: a toy box says "batteries not included" or "each sold separately"
column3: read the small print before asking for it
column4: the extra parts can cost more money

column2: cereals with cartoon characters are on low shelves in the supermarket
column3: know this is on purpose, at children's eye level
column4: shops and companies want children to ask parents to buy them

column2: a fast-food meal comes with a free toy
column3: know the toy is there to make you want the meal
column4: the "free" toy is part of the price and the selling plan

column2: an advert says "up to 70% off"
column3: know "up to" means only a few things are that cheap
column4: big numbers grab attention, but most items have smaller discounts

column2: a price is $9.99 or £4.99 instead of 10 or 5
column3: know it is almost the same as the round number
column4: shops use these prices because they look cheaper than they are

column2: a famous YouTuber or influencer loves a product
column3: look for #ad, "sponsored" or "paid partnership"
column4: influencers are often paid to praise products

column2: a game is "free" but keeps offering gems, coins or loot boxes for real money
column3: never buy in-app items without a parent's permission
column4: free games earn money from small purchases that add up fast

column2: a loot box in a game could give a rare prize
column3: know it is like gambling: you pay without knowing what you get
column4: games make it exciting so that you spend more

column2: burgers in adverts look much bigger and shinier than real ones
column3: know food in adverts is styled and photographed to look perfect
column4: real food is usually smaller and messier

column2: an advert says "9 out of 10 dentists recommend"
column3: ask how many were asked and who paid for the survey
column4: numbers in adverts may come from small or chosen groups

column2: an advert says "Hurry, only today!" with a countdown
column3: take your time; real bargains rarely disappear in minutes
column4: rushing people stops them thinking clearly

column2: a product says "new and improved"
column3: ask what has actually changed
column4: it may be just a new box to make you buy again

column2: a character in a film drinks a well-known brand of soda
column3: know this is product placement: companies pay to show their products
column4: it is advertising hidden inside entertainment

column2: a cereal box says "part of a balanced breakfast" or "with real fruit"
column3: look at the sugar on the label with an adult
column4: words on the front can make sugary food sound healthier than it is

column2: an advert says "results may vary" or "*not typical" in small writing
column3: know this means most people will not get the shown results
column4: the tiny writing is where the true limits are

column2: you want something just because everyone has it
column3: wait a few days and see if you still want it
column4: adverts and friends create a feeling that fades, and waiting helps you choose wisely

column2: a message says you have won a free iPhone but must click and enter details
column3: do not click; close it and tell an adult
column4: you cannot win a contest you never entered; it is a trick to steal information or money

column2: a website offers free Robux, V-Bucks or game coins
column3: never use "generators" or give your password for free coins
column4: they are scams that steal accounts or install harmful software

column2: someone online offers to trade a rare game item if you give yours first
column3: only use official in-game trading, never trade outside the game
column4: many trades are scams where you give and get nothing back

column2: a stranger says you can earn lots of money quickly
column3: know that real money takes real work; ignore and tell an adult
column4: get rich quick offers are almost always tricks

column2: expensive trainers are on sale for a tiny price on a strange website
column3: ask a parent to check it; it may be fake or never arrive
column4: fake shops copy brand names and steal card details

column2: a pop-up says "Congratulations, you are the 1,000,000th visitor!"
column3: close the page without clicking
column4: this is a classic scam pop-up shown to everyone

column2: a "free trial" asks for a parent's card number
column3: always ask a parent first
column4: free trials often turn into paid subscriptions if not cancelled

column2: a chain message says forward it to 10 friends to get a prize
column3: do not forward it
column4: no company gives prizes for chain messages; they just spread

column2: a chain message says something bad will happen if you don't forward it
column3: ignore and delete it; nothing bad will happen
column4: it is a trick to frighten people into spreading it

column2: a sweet-looking stranger offers sweets or a puppy to come with them
column3: never go anywhere with someone you do not know; run to a safe adult
column4: offers of treats are a known trick to lure children

column2: someone you met in a game asks for your password
column3: never share your password with anyone except your parent or carer
column4: anyone with your password can take over your account

column2: an email "from your bank" or "from Apple" says click to fix your account
column3: do not click links in such messages; show an adult
column4: fake messages copy real logos to trick people (called phishing)

column2: a text says a parcel could not be delivered, click here
column3: do not click; adults check deliveries on the official site
column4: parcel texts are a very common scam

column2: a pop-up says "Virus detected! Call this number"
column3: close the page and tell an adult; never call the number
column4: real computers do not warn you through web pop-ups with phone numbers

column2: a friend's account suddenly asks you to buy gift cards for them
column3: talk to your friend another way, like in person or by phone
column4: their account may be hacked, and gift card requests are a classic scam

column2: someone asks you to pay with gift cards or game cards
column3: know that real businesses never ask to be paid with gift cards
column4: scammers like gift cards because they cannot be traced or refunded

column2: a person online says they are 10 but asks to keep chats secret from your parents
column3: stop chatting and tell a trusted adult
column4: people online may not be who they say, and asking for secrecy is a warning sign

column2: an online friend asks for photos of you or your home
column3: never send photos, your address or school to people you only know online
column4: they can be used to find you or to harm you

column2: an online contact asks you to move to a private app or to meet up
column3: say no and tell a parent
column4: moving away from watched places and meeting up are danger signs

column2: someone online threatens to share something unless you send more
column3: do not reply or send anything; tell a trusted adult right away; it is not your fault
column4: adults and police can help; in the UK you can report to CEOP, in the USA to the NCMEC CyberTipline, in Australia to the eSafety Commissioner, in New Zealand to Netsafe

column2: a message pretends to be from a famous YouTuber giving away money
column3: check the real account and do not send anything
column4: scammers create fake celebrity accounts with similar names

column2: a phone caller says they are from the government and your family owes money
column3: do not give any information; give the phone to a parent
column4: real officials do not demand money by surprise calls

column2: a parent gets a text "Hi Mum, I've lost my phone, this is my new number, send money"
column3: know this is a common scam; families can agree a check question or code word
column4: scammers pretend to be children to trick parents

column2: a QR code on a poster offers a prize
column3: ask an adult before scanning unknown codes
column4: QR codes can lead to fake websites

column2: an app asks for permission to use your contacts, camera and location
column3: ask a parent and only allow what the app really needs
column4: apps can collect and sell your information

column2: a website looks almost like a real one but the address is misspelled
column3: check the address carefully, like "amaz0n" instead of "amazon"
column4: fake sites copy real ones with tiny spelling changes

column2: a free download of a paid game
column3: do not download games from unofficial sites
column4: they often carry viruses or steal information

column2: someone you don't know sends you a friend request
column3: only accept people you know in real life
column4: strangers can pretend to be anyone

column2: you clicked a scam link by mistake
column3: tell a parent straight away; you will not be in trouble for being honest
column4: changing passwords quickly can stop the damage

column2: someone says you will be arrested unless you pay
column3: know this is a scare scam; tell a parent
column4: real police do not ask for payment by message or phone

column2: a shocking headline in big capital letters
column3: read beyond the headline and check other sources
column4: headlines are written to make you click and can be misleading

column2: a post says "share this before it gets deleted!"
column3: be suspicious and do not share it
column4: this phrase is a trick to make false stories spread fast

column2: a photo shows a shark swimming on a flooded motorway
column3: ask an adult to help do a reverse image search
column4: edited and fake photos often spread after big events

column2: a picture of a person has strange hands with extra fingers or blurry writing
column3: know it may be made by AI
column4: AI images can look real but often have small mistakes

column2: a video shows a famous person saying something odd
column3: know videos and voices can be faked (deepfakes); check trusted news sources
column4: technology can make people seem to say things they never said

column2: a news story is shared as new but is from years ago
column3: check the date
column4: old stories are often reshared as if they just happened

column2: a story comes from a funny news website like The Onion
column3: know some sites write satire: made-up news as jokes
column4: satire is not lying when readers know it is a joke, but it can fool people who don't

column2: a fact on a website with no author and no sources
column3: trust sites that say who wrote them and where facts come from
column4: anyone can write anything online

column2: you are not sure if something is true
column3: check whether two or three reliable sources say the same
column4: true important news is usually reported by many trusted outlets

column2: someone says a fact is true "because it's on the internet"
column3: know the internet has true and false things side by side
column4: being online does not make something true

column2: a video says the Earth is flat
column3: know scientists have shown the Earth is round in many ways, including photos from space
column4: some videos spread ideas that are wrong, even if they sound confident

column2: a statement is someone's opinion, like "Pizza is the best food"
column3: learn to tell fact (can be checked) from opinion (what someone thinks)
column4: both are fine, but opinions should not be passed off as facts

column2: a "news" story makes you very angry or scared
column3: stop and check before sharing
column4: false stories are often designed to stir up strong feelings

column2: a post says "doctors hate this one trick!"
column3: know this is clickbait selling something
column4: real medical advice comes from doctors and health services, not tricks

column2: you read a Wikipedia article for homework
column3: use it to start, and check the references at the bottom
column4: anyone can edit Wikipedia, so sources make facts stronger

column2: an account posts many messages repeating the same thing
column3: know some accounts are bots or fake accounts
column4: they make an idea look more popular than it is

column2: a friend says a famous person died but it isn't on the news
column3: wait for trusted news before believing or sharing
column4: celebrity death hoaxes are common

column2: a post says drinking something cures every illness
column3: know a "cure for everything" is a myth; ask a doctor
column4: real medicines are tested carefully and work for specific problems

column2: friends dare you to eat something gross or unsafe
column3: say "No thanks" and change the subject
column4: you don't have to prove anything; your health matters more than a dare

column2: someone dares you to jump from a high wall or roof
column3: say no and walk away
column4: falls can cause broken bones or worse, and friends who matter won't want you hurt

column2: someone dares you to run across a road in front of cars
column3: never do it
column4: traffic can kill in a second; no dare is worth that risk

column2: friends say "Everyone's doing it"
column3: remember that "everyone" is rarely true, and you can decide for yourself
column4: people often follow a crowd without thinking whether it is right

column2: a friend wants you to take sweets from a shop without paying
column3: say no and leave
column4: it is stealing, it is against the law, and the shop and its workers lose out

column2: older kids offer you a vape or cigarette
column3: say no and tell a trusted adult
column4: nicotine is addictive and harmful to growing bodies, and selling it to children is illegal

column2: you are dared to touch an electric fence or climb an electricity pylon
column3: never do it
column4: electricity can kill instantly

column2: friends pressure you to leave someone out of the game
column3: invite them in or play with them yourself
column4: it takes courage to be kind when others aren't, and it matters a lot to the left-out child

column2: a dare from an online "challenge" video
column3: never try challenges involving choking, holding breath, medicines, fire or eating things like detergent pods
column4: such challenges have hurt and killed children

column2: you want to say no but feel embarrassed
column3: use an easy excuse like "My parents would ground me forever"
column4: blaming parents is an accepted way to escape pressure, and parents are happy to be the excuse

column2: you are at a friend's house and feel unsafe or pressured
column3: use a family code word or text to get picked up
column4: families can agree a secret word that means "come and get me, no questions asked"

column2: friends call you "chicken" for not doing a dare
column3: know that saying no takes more courage than following
column4: standing firm earns real respect over time

column2: a friend pressures you into skipping a lesson
column3: stay in class
column4: it gets you in trouble and worries school staff who must know where you are

column2: positive peer pressure: friends encourage you to join a team or try a new food
column3: give it a try if it is safe
column4: peer pressure can also be good when it helps you grow

column2: a friend tells you they are planning a surprise for their mum
column3: keep it; it's a good secret
column4: surprises end happily and nobody gets hurt

column2: an adult asks you to keep a secret from your parents
column3: tell your parents or another trusted adult
column4: safe adults do not ask children to keep secrets from their parents

column2: someone touches you in a way that feels wrong and says "it's our secret"
column3: tell a trusted adult as soon as you can; it is never your fault
column4: secrets about touching are never okay to keep, and trusted adults will help

column2: a friend tells you someone at home is hurting them
column3: tell a trusted adult like a teacher, even if your friend asked you not to
column4: your friend needs help that only adults can give

column2: a friend says they want to hurt themselves
column3: tell a trusted adult right away
column4: this is too big for a child to handle alone; getting help shows real friendship

column2: you know the difference between surprises and secrets
column3: remember: surprises are happy and get told soon; secrets that make you worried or scared should be told
column4: this simple rule helps you decide what to share

column2: a friend shares that they wet the bed sometimes
column3: keep it private
column4: it is personal and not harmful; sharing it would embarrass them

column2: your password
column3: keep it secret from friends; share only with your parents or carers
column4: it protects your accounts and you

column2: a friend tells you a secret and you accidentally tell someone
column3: say sorry to your friend honestly
column4: owning up helps repair the trust

column2: someone tells you a secret about who is being picked on
column3: tell an adult so they can stop the bullying
column4: bullying gets worse when it stays hidden

column2: a friend is planning to run away
column3: tell a trusted adult
column4: running away can be very dangerous, and something may be wrong that adults can help fix

column2: a friend shows you a weapon or says they will bring one to school
column3: tell an adult right away
column4: it is a danger to everyone, and adults must know immediately

column2: you keep a diary
column3: it's fine to keep your thoughts private
column4: everyone has a right to private thoughts

column2: you find out a family secret, like a present for Christmas
column3: keep quiet and act surprised
column4: spoiling a present takes the joy from the giver

column2: you knock over a vase and it breaks
column3: tell an adult straight away and say sorry
column4: owning up shows responsibility, and adults are usually less upset about honesty than about lies

column2: you lose a library book
column3: tell the librarian; you may need to pay or replace it
column4: libraries are shared, and honesty lets the problem be fixed

column2: your bike scratches a parked car
column3: find the owner or tell your parents
column4: the owner deserves to know, and running away makes it much worse

column2: you forget your homework
column3: tell the teacher honestly before they ask
column4: making up excuses usually gets noticed and causes more trouble

column2: you accidentally hurt a friend in a game
column3: stop, check if they are okay and say sorry
column4: caring about someone you hurt matters more than whose fault it was

column2: you break a friend's toy while borrowing it
column3: tell them, say sorry and offer to fix or replace it
column4: taking responsibility keeps the friendship

column2: you spill juice on the carpet
column3: tell an adult right away so it can be cleaned
column4: stains are easier to clean quickly, and hiding it can ruin the carpet

column2: you ate the last biscuit that was saved for someone else
column3: own up and say sorry
column4: small honesty shows you are trustworthy in big things too

column2: your brother got blamed for something you did
column3: tell the truth and clear his name
column4: letting someone else take the blame is unfair

column2: your ball breaks a neighbour's window
column3: go with a parent to the neighbour, say sorry and offer to help pay
column4: neighbours appreciate honesty, and it keeps good relations

column2: you lose a jacket a friend lent you
column3: tell them quickly and help to find it or replace it
column4: waiting makes it harder to find and harder to explain

column2: how to say a good sorry
column3: say what you did, that you are sorry, and how you will make it right
column4: a real apology names the mistake and tries to fix it

column2: someone apologises to you
column3: accept it kindly and try to move on
column4: forgiveness helps both people feel better

column2: you said something mean when you were angry
column3: go back later and apologise
column4: words can hurt even after the anger has gone

column2: you lied before and your parents check up on you more now
column3: keep telling the truth and trust will grow back slowly
column4: trust is quick to lose and slow to rebuild

column2: you are given a house key for the first time
column3: keep it safe and never tell strangers where it is or that you are home alone
column4: it shows your parents trust you to be responsible

column2: you are sent to the shop with money
column3: bring back the right change and receipt
column4: being careful with money shows you can be trusted

column2: a teacher leaves the class for a moment
column3: behave as if they were there
column4: being good when no one is watching is what makes you trustworthy

column2: you are asked to look after a younger sibling for a few minutes
column3: keep them in sight and call an adult if anything happens
column4: someone small depends on you

column2: a friend lends you their favourite book
column3: take care of it and return it on time
column4: caring for others' things shows respect

column2: you are the class monitor for a day
column3: do the job fairly, not favouring friends
column4: fairness makes others respect your role

column2: a neighbour asks you to water their plants while they are away
column3: do it every day as agreed and don't touch other things
column4: people trust you with their home

column2: you are told the story "The Boy Who Cried Wolf"
column3: remember that people who lie are not believed even when they tell the truth
column4: honesty protects you when you need help

column2: you promised to keep a friend's secret and kept it
column3: know that keeping safe secrets makes people trust you more
column4: trust is built in small moments

column2: you find a wallet on the street
column3: give it to a parent or the police so it can be returned
column4: the owner may need the money and cards, and keeping it is wrong and can be illegal

column2: you find money on the school floor
column3: take it to the school office or a teacher
column4: the owner may come looking for it

column2: you find a phone on a bus
column3: hand it to the driver or lost property
column4: phones are precious, and the owner will check there

column2: someone says "finders keepers, losers weepers"
column3: know this is a playground rhyme, not a rule; return things when you can find the owner
column4: the owner did not give it away; they lost it

column2: a shop assistant gives you too much change
column3: tell them and give it back
column4: the assistant may have to pay the difference, and honesty matters even when it costs you

column2: a vending machine gives you two snacks instead of one
column3: tell the shop or school if it is theirs
column4: the extra snack was paid for by someone else

column2: you find the answers to tomorrow's test
column3: do not look; give them to the teacher
column4: using them would be cheating and unfair to the class

column2: you find a friend's diary
column3: do not read it; give it back
column4: reading private writing breaks trust

column2: you find someone's password written down
column3: do not use it; tell them so they can change it
column4: using someone's account without permission is wrong and can be against the law

column2: you find a toy in the park
column3: leave it where it was or take it to lost property
column4: the owner may come back to look for it

column2: you find a lost dog with a tag
column3: tell an adult who can call the number; a vet can scan a microchip
column4: owners love their pets and are worried

column2: you find money in a second-hand book or coat
column3: ask an adult; it may be returned to the seller or donated
column4: it belongs to someone else

column2: you find a coin on the pavement with nobody around
column3: tell an adult; very small sums with no way to find the owner may be kept, but bigger finds should be handed in
column4: the rule is to make a real effort to find the owner, and that is easier with larger things

column2: a friend wants to keep something they found that you know belongs to a classmate
column3: encourage them to give it back
column4: returning things makes your class a place where people trust each other

column2: someone accuses you of taking something you didn't
column3: stay calm, tell the truth and ask an adult to help
column4: calm honesty is the best answer to a false accusation

column2: sharing out sweets among friends
column3: share fairly and offer first to others
column4: fairness keeps friendships strong
